## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Tacchasūkarajātaka* (Ja 492) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection, published as the ninth story in the fourth volume of V. Fausböll’s edition [Fausböll 1887]. According to the traditional introductory setting, the Buddha related this story while staying at the Jetavana monastery regarding two ancient elders, opening with the verse line, “I wandered, searching far” [SuttaCentral].
The frame narrative shares elements with the *Vaḍḍhakisūkarajātaka*, recounting the historical hostilities between King Ajātasattu and King Pasenadi of Kosala [Radich 2011]. This dispute arose following the death of Queen Vaidehī over a Kāsi revenue village (*Kāsigāma*) originally granted to her as bath-money (*nahānīyamūlatthāya*) by King Mahākosala upon her marriage to Bimbisāra [Fausböll 1887; Radich 2011]. Within the commentary, King Pasenadi receives practical strategic advice for battle rather than traditional incantations [Rhys Davids 1917]. In the story’s identification (*samodhāna*), the treacherous ascetic is identified with Devadatta, the carpenter's boar (*tacchasūkaro*) with the elder Dhanuggahatissa—who had expertise in battle arrays—and the tree devatā (*rukkhadevatā*) with the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1887].
While SuttaCentral does not record curated cross-canonical parallels, DharmaNexus detects automated alignments with two segments of the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (*Zhong ahan jing*, T 26) [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus also records extensive Pali-internal text reuse with the fourth volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, comprising 19 matching passages spanning over 3,200 shared characters [DharmaNexus].
